questions.q: Why not just fit ordinary linear regression to a 0/1 "defaulted" target?
options: Because linear regression cannot use debt-to-income as a feature
Because linear regression is too slow on binary data
Because linear regression always predicts exactly 0 or 1
Because a straight line can output values below 0 and above 1 (−0.16 and 1.28 on the twelve applicants), which cannot be probabilities
questions.why: The straight line has the wrong shape for probabilities: it runs off below 0 and above 1. Logistic regression keeps the weighted sum but bends it through the sigmoid, which always lies between 0 and 1. Speed is not the issue, and a line does not output only 0s and 1s, which is precisely the problem.

questions.q: A customer has a predicted churn probability of **0.9**. What are the **odds** of churn?
questions.why: Odds = p / (1 − p) = 0.9 / 0.1 = 9, "nine to one on". 0.9 confuses odds with probability, and 0.11 is the odds of **not** churning (0.1 / 0.9). Odds and probability are close only when p is small.

questions.q: Using the twelve-applicant model **z = −5.54 + 1.16 × DTI** (DTI in tenths), what is the predicted probability of default for an applicant with DTI **0.4**?
options: About 0.71
About 0.29
About 0.40
questions.why: z = −5.54 + 1.16 × 4 = −0.90, and p = 1 / (1 + e^0.90) ≈ 0.29. −0.90 is the score (log-odds), not a probability. 0.71 is σ(+0.90), from dropping the minus sign. 0.40 just repeats the DTI value.

questions.q: A customer **repaid** (y = 0), but the model gave them a **0.8** probability of default. What is the log-loss for this case?
options: About 1.61
About 0.22
About 0.80
questions.why: For y = 0 the cost is −ln(1 − p) = −ln 0.2 ≈ 1.61. 0.22 is −ln 0.8, the cost you would pay if the customer had defaulted. Log-loss is not the raw probability error; the logarithm is what makes confident mistakes expensive.

questions.q: At a 0.5 threshold, out of 1,000 applicants (100 defaulters), the model catches 55 defaulters, misses 45 and wrongly declines 30 good customers. Which reading is correct?
options: Recall is 55% and precision is about 65%
Recall is about 65% and precision is 55%
Recall is 55% and precision is 30%
Accuracy is 55%
questions.why: Recall = caught / all defaulters = 55 / 100 = 55%. Precision = caught / all declined = 55 / (55 + 30) ≈ 65%. Swapping the two is the most common slip. Accuracy is (55 + 870) / 1,000 = 92.5%, not 55%.

questions.q: Approving a defaulter costs **₹1,50,000**; declining a good customer loses **₹30,000** of profit. If the probabilities are well calibrated, above what predicted default probability should the bank decline?
options: About 0.17
About 0.83
questions.why: Break-even threshold = cost of a false decline / (cost of a false decline + cost of a missed defaulter) = 30,000 / (30,000 + 1,50,000) ≈ 0.17. 0.20 is 30,000 / 1,50,000, which forgets to add the two costs. 0.83 puts the wrong cost on top. 0.5 only makes sense when both mistakes cost the same.

questions.q: One feature splits your training data perfectly: every applicant with DTI above 0.6 defaulted and every one below repaid. What happens to an unpenalised logistic regression?
options: It fits a sensible, finite coefficient with probability 0.5 at DTI 0.6
It switches automatically to a decision tree
The coefficient becomes zero because there is no error left to reduce
The coefficient grows without limit as the optimiser keeps sharpening the S-curve; a penalty (on by default in scikit-learn) keeps it finite
questions.why: With perfect separation, a steeper sigmoid always lowers log-loss a little more, so the best coefficient is infinite. scikit-learn's default L2 penalty (`C=1.0`) prevents this. The intuition that "no error means nothing to fit" is backwards: log-loss can always be pushed closer to zero by more confident predictions.

questions.q: Interview question: "At the 0.2 threshold your model is 83% accurate, but approving everyone would be 90% accurate. Is your model worse?"
options: Yes: higher accuracy always means a better model
Yes, so the threshold should be raised back to 0.5
No: with 10% defaulters, approving everyone catches none of them; the 0.2 model costs ₹70 lakh against ₹2 crore for approve-all, so judge by business cost, recall, precision and AUC, not accuracy
No, because accuracy cannot be computed for logistic regression
questions.why: On imbalanced data, accuracy rewards ignoring the rare class. Approving all 1,000 misses 100 defaulters at ₹2 lakh each (₹2 crore), whereas the 0.2 threshold costs 20 × ₹2L + 150 × ₹0.2L = ₹70 lakh. Precision, recall, ROC-AUC and expected cost measure what the bank actually cares about.
